title: Eighteen Digits, Ones and Twos
statement: How many $18$-digit positive integers have every digit equal to $1$ or $2$ and are divisible by each of $7$, $11$ and $13$?
hints: Multiply $7$, $11$ and $13$. Then cut the $18$-digit number into six blocks of three digits.

Since $7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 = 1001$ and $1000 \equiv -1 \pmod{1001}$, the number is divisible by $1001$ exactly when the alternating sum of its six three-digit blocks is. Each block lies between $111$ and $222$, which makes this alternating sum small.

The alternating sum lies between $-333$ and $333$, so it must be $0$: the first, third and fifth blocks have the same total as the other three. Adding three blocks produces no carries, so compare the hundreds, the tens and the units separately.
solution:
Split the number into three-digit blocks $G_1, G_2, \dots, G_6$, from the right. Since $7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 = 1001$ and $1000 \equiv -1 \pmod{1001}$, the number is divisible by all three primes exactly when $1001$ divides $S = G_1 - G_2 + G_3 - G_4 + G_5 - G_6$. Each block is between $111$ and $222$, so $|S| \le 666 - 333 = 333 < 1001$. Hence $S = 0$, that is, $G_1 + G_3 + G_5 = G_2 + G_4 + G_6$.

In a sum of three blocks each column adds three digits equal to $1$ or $2$, which is at most $6$, so there are no carries. The equation therefore holds exactly when the hundreds, the tens and the units columns agree separately. In one column, the three digits from $G_1, G_3, G_5$ must contain as many $2$s as the three from $G_2, G_4, G_6$, which happens in $\binom{3}{0}^2 + \binom{3}{1}^2 + \binom{3}{2}^2 + \binom{3}{3}^2 = 20$ ways. The columns are independent, so the answer is $20^3 = 8000$.
